extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in 19th-century maritime history and ship design (historians, sailors, enthusiasts)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and metrics used to assess the design, construction, and operational performance of mid-19th-century emigrant clippers (e.g., Sovereign of the Seas, Lightning, Red Jacket), including measurements, sailing performance, seaworthiness, and passenger accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tonnage and principal dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of keel, length between perpendiculars, overall length, beam, depth, and registered/burthen tonnage as primary descriptors of a ship (e.g., Sovereign of the Seas: length over all 265 ft; beam 44 ft; depth 23 ft; tonnage 2421 tons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these measurements to compare size and carrying capacity; tables of port-to-port passages use anchor-to-anchor times in conjunction with these dimensions to evaluate passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sail area (yards of canvas spread)
rubrics_metrics.description: Total canvas spread in working suit (e.g., Sovereign of the Seas spread 12,000 yards; Lightning 13,000 yards under all plain sail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger sail area indicates potential power and speed; compare with spars/mast dimensions and crew capability to judge practical carrying of sail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spar and mast dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Diameters and lengths of masts and yards (e.g., James Baines' mainmast 42 in diameter; mainyard 26 in; Lightning's mainmast deck to truck 164 ft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavier/thicker spars and tall masts correlate with ability to carry extensive canvas and withstand heavy weather; specific diameters cited as evidence of robustness aloft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigging quality and staying (strength of gear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the best available standing rigging (e.g., 11½ inch Russian hemp for Lightning's lower rigging), scientifically stayed masts and robust outfit to reduce dismasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should examine materials, rope thickness, and staying patterns; 'no ships were more scientifically stayed than these big ships' is treated as a positive design indicator against spar loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigging technique (topsails roped diagonally etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific rigging practices such as diagonally roping topsails, topgallants and royals from clew to earing to secure canvas in heavy conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovations in rigging technique that reduce sail loss and improve control are evaluated favorably; examples from logs show these practices enabled heavy-weather sail carrying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beam-to-length ratio (hull proportions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beams-to-length ratios used to compare national/builders' tendencies (e.g., Lightning 5.54 beams to length, Marco Polo 4.86 beams to length).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ratio to infer form: wider hulls (higher beam ratio) vs. longer, finer hulls affect steadiness, cargo/passenger space and speed; compare across American, British, Nova Scotian builds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hull form and lines (design geometry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative hull features: concave water-lines, raked stem, semi-elliptical stern, long clean after-body—features that define sharpness, run, and seaworthiness (e.g., Lightning described as 'one of the sharpest ships ever launched').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate model/lines for how they blend speed (fine bow, clean run) with sea-kindliness; textual descriptions and designer notes used as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction materials and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of hull materials and construction (e.g., Sobraon built of finest Malabar teak and with iron frames retained speed; comparison between wooden and iron-framed ships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material choice (teak, iron frames) and workmanship are indicators of durability and long-term performance; note tradeoffs in weight, stiffness and longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Load line and freeboard (light load line and high side)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ships sailed on a lighter load line and showed a higher side, making them dry, buoyant and steady (passengers could dance on the poop at 15–16 knots).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher freeboard and lighter loading improve dryness and comfort; evaluate how passenger numbers and cargo stowage affect seaworthiness and habitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seaworthiness and steadiness in a seaway
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative evidence of steady behavior and lack of violent rolling (logs and passenger testimony stating ships were 'dry and buoyant' and able to be danced on at high speeds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logbook anecdotes and passenger/observer testimony to assess motions and comfort; corroborate with 24-hour run data where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to carry sail in heavy weather
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity to keep royals, skysails, studding sails set and still make high speeds in gales (numerous log entries: ships carrying main skysail and topgallant studding sails while doing 16–21 knots).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sail-carrying decisions in logs relative to sea state and wind; sustained heavy-sail carriage is a marker of hull/rig strength and seamanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: 24-hour runs and extraordinary day runs
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance covered in 24 hours used as a performance metric (e.g., Lightning 436 nautical miles, James Baines 423 nm), with lists of all verified runs of 400 miles and over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat verified 24-hour runs and multi-day averages as primary empirical evidence of speed; require trustworthy noon positions/observations for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passage times (anchor-to-anchor/dock-to-anchorage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Total passage durations between ports (e.g., Honolulu to New York 82 days; New York to Liverpool 13 days 22 hours 50 minutes), often presented in tables for comparative performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anchor-to-anchor or dock-to-anchorage times for fair comparisons; note seasonal and route variations when judging 'record' passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and trustworthiness of navigation records
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliability of logbook observations and noon positions; criticisms of 'reckoning 60 miles to a degree' vs. verified observation (e.g., Captain Enright's letter asserting degrees equalled 44 miles and providing noon positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer corroborated astronomical observations and multiple positions for validating claimed runs; guard against systematic overstatement practices in historical sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crew composition and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate numbers and roles in the crew (e.g., 105 men and boys including bosuns, carpenters, sailmakers, stewards, cooks) and the effect of crew quality on operations and discipline (mutiny suppression anecdote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether crew complements and senior officers' competence supported the ship's performance and safety; desertion or insufficient clothing/health can impair performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onboard fittings and passenger accommodation
rubrics_metrics.description: Saloon, poop and 'tween deck heights and other luxuries (e.g., Lightning poop 92 ft, saloon 86 ft, 8 ft under beams) that improved passenger comfort on long voyages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate passenger spaces for space per person, headroom, and amenities; such features affected emigrant experience and could influence a ship's reputation/trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisioning innovations (water tanks and stores)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel provisions such as iron water tanks holding large capacities (Lightning's 36,000 gallons) as improvements for long voyages and passenger service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisioning capacity and systems are operational criteria — larger, well-designed stores reduce risk on long passages and improve habitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to dismasting and aloft casualties
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidence of carrying away spars and sails deemed rare among the best-built clippers due to learned design; 'the carrying away of spars and sails... was quite rare on these big emigrant ships.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low rates of spar loss and dismasting historically signal superior design and outfitting; evaluate against rigging, staying and seamanship records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logbook detail as evidence (winds, barometer, positions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed daily log entries (wind direction/force, barometer, noon positions, runs) used as the evidentiary basis for performance claims and to rebut skepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full logbook context (weather, course changes) to interpret large runs; isolated distance claims should be corroborated with positions and weather entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tradeoffs (strength vs. beauty vs. cargo trade)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of design choices that favour 'powerful workmanlike appearance' (Donald Mackay) vs. 'graceful curves' (Red Jacket), and whether ships were optimized for specific trades (too big for San Francisco/China trades).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess design in light of intended trade and route; aesthetic descriptions often accompany functional assessments—weight design against intended service and performance results.
